trn.update.title: Training: one visible weight update
trn.update.intro: Next-token training minimizes −ln p(correct token). The backward pass computes gradients: how does the loss change when a weight changes? The optimizer uses them to update the weights; inference normally does not.
trn.update.formula: Isolate the mechanism with a toy loss: L(w) = ½(w − 3)², g = dL/dw = w − 3. One SGD step is w′ = w − ηg. η is the learning rate.
trn.update.example: Start at w = 1: g = −2 and L = 2. With η = 0.5, w′ = 2 and L(w′) = 0.5. A negative gradient therefore makes the weight increase.
trn.update.predict: Predict first: what happens at η = 1, 2 and 2.5? Move the slider. Each setting shows one step from the same start, not repeated training.
trn.update.caveat: This one-dimensional parabola is not a language model’s loss landscape. Real training uses minibatches, many interacting weights and often AdamW; a better training step does not guarantee better results on new data.
trn.update.aria: Loss curve with the starting weight, gradient step and updated weight
trn.update.higher: Loss increases: the step is too large.
trn.stages.title: Pretraining and SFT: different data
trn.stages.intro: Both stages can use next-token cross-entropy. The difference is mainly which sequences and target positions the model learns from, not that SFT replaces language modeling with a new kind of intelligence.
trn.stages.pre.title: Pretraining: a broad text distribution
trn.stages.pre.data: Large, curated text collections teach linguistic patterns and many associations. Licensing, personal data, duplicates and data quality matter.
trn.stages.pre.example: Text: “Water freezes at …” → next token. Under teacher forcing, each position receives the actual preceding text, not the model’s own previous guess.
trn.stages.pre.loss: Loss is summed or averaged over selected valid target positions. Padding should not count as ordinary text.
trn.stages.sft.title: SFT: demonstrations of desired behavior
trn.stages.sft.data: Supervised fine-tuning uses, for example, instruction–response pairs and multi-turn dialogs with a specific chat template. The model still trains to predict the target text’s tokens.
trn.stages.sft.example: Instruction: “Explain freezing briefly.” → assistant response. Instruction tokens are often masked out of the loss but remain as context. The exact mask depends on the training recipe.
trn.stages.sft.loss: Chat format and examples teach response style and instruction following. Full fine-tuning can change all weights; adapter training changes a smaller parameter set.
trn.stages.separate: Split documents, users or task families before training when needed to prevent leakage. Training data updates weights, validation data selects the recipe, and an untouched test set estimates generalization.
trn.stages.caveat: Neither pretraining nor SFT guarantees factual correctness. Fine-tuning can also learn new domain information, memorize data or degrade earlier capabilities; test both the target domain and regressions.
trn.pref.title: Preferences: RLHF and DPO
trn.pref.pair: The same prompt x gets two responses: y+ is chosen and y− rejected by a rater. The label expresses a comparative preference in these data, not proof that y+ is true.
trn.pref.rlhf: A common RLHF pipeline first learns a reward model from comparisons and then optimizes a policy against that reward. A KL penalty against a reference policy can limit drift; its strength and direction depend on the recipe.
trn.pref.dpo: DPO trains directly on pairs with a frozen reference policy πref, without a separate reward model or RL loop in the standard recipe. The log ratios compare change relative to the reference, not just which response was already most likely.
trn.pref.formula: m = ln[πθ(y+|x)/πref(y+|x)] − ln[πθ(y−|x)/πref(y−|x)]. L_DPO = −ln σ(βm) = ln(1 + exp(−βm)). These are sequence probabilities, with masking defined by the recipe.
trn.pref.caveat: β > 0 participates in the connection to a KL-regularized ideal objective; β in this fixed-margin view does not by itself show how far a trained policy drifts. DPO is not the same as explicitly adding KL to each displayed loss. Noise, bias and reward hacking remain.
trn.pref.aria: Modeled preference probability and DPO loss as the margin changes
trn.pref.out: m = {{m}}; β = {{beta}}; σ(βm) = {{p}}; L_DPO = {{loss}}. At m = 0, loss is ln 2 ≈ 0.693.
trn.pref.readout: The bars are a modeled preference between two responses, not their generation probabilities or a truth meter. A higher margin lowers this pair’s loss; more pairs and evaluation are needed.
trn.lora.title: LoRA: frozen base and low rank
trn.lora.intro: Freeze the base matrix W and learn two smaller matrices A and B. The adapter adds a change to the same linear projection, not extra tokens to the prompt.
trn.lora.formula: With row vectors: y = xW + (α/r)(xA)B. x: [1, 6], W: [6, 4], A: [6, r], B: [r, 4], y: [1, 4]. Here α = r so that α/r = 1.
trn.lora.shapes: xA has shape [1, r]; (xA)B has [1, 4] and can be added to xW. Libraries using column vectors sometimes reverse the names A and B or transpose them.
trn.lora.rank: The update AB has rank at most r. In this miniature model the base has 24 parameters and the adapter 10r. For large projections and small r the fraction is small; in our tiny example the adapter can exceed the base.
trn.lora.caveat: Low rank limits the update’s matrix rank, not which facts can be learned. Rank, selected projections and data affect results; parameter counts imply no general quality guarantee.
trn.lora.aria: Two parallel paths: a frozen base matrix and trainable low-rank matrices
trn.lora.out: r = {{r}}: A has {{a}} and B has {{b}} parameters; {{n}} trainable in total versus 24 frozen. xA: [1, {{r}}] → (xA)B: [1, 4].
trn.qlora.title: QLoRA: what has which precision?
trn.qlora.intro: QLoRA combines a frozen, quantized base with trainable LoRA adapters. Quantized storage and compute precision are different questions. The original recipe’s NF4 is not the same uniform integer quantization as the next module’s experiment. Quantization stores the weights in fewer bits; dequantization turns a stored code back into an approximate value when it is used.
trn.qlora.base.precision: For example, 4-bit NF4 with scale metadata
trn.qlora.base.update: Frozen; no optimizer update of the base weights
trn.qlora.adapter.precision: Higher precision, for example bf16; recipe-dependent
trn.qlora.adapter.update: Gradients and optimizer steps for the adapters
trn.qlora.compute.update: Activations are needed for backward; state follows trainable parameters
trn.qlora.flow: The computation can be written y = x·dequant(Wq) + (α/r)(xA)B. Dequantization can occur in kernel blocks, not necessarily as a whole extra matrix in memory. Gradients can pass through computations with frozen weights to trainable adapters.
trn.qlora.memory: Base storage shrinks, but activations, adapters, optimizer state and temporary buffers remain. At inference the adapter may stay separate or be merged with dequantized weights; requantizing after merging can add error.
trn.qlora.caveat: Full model quantization comes next. QLoRA does not mean all training operations run in 4-bit or that every task matches full fine-tuning quality.
ql.scale.title: Scale, zero point and rounding
ql.scale.intro: Quantization replaces values with a finite set of codes. Dequantization reconstructs an approximation: x̂ = s(q − z), with scale s > 0 and integer zero point z. Fewer bits mean coarser steps over the same range.
ql.scale.symmetric: Symmetric here: Q = 2^(b−1) − 1, q ∈ [−Q, Q], s = 2/Q, z = 0. q = clamp(round(x/s), −Q, Q). The range is [−2, 2]; the most negative signed code is unused. At 2 bits there are therefore 3 used levels.
ql.scale.affine: Affine here: l = −1, u = 3, Q = 2^b − 1, s = (u − l)/Q, z = clamp(round(−l/s), 0, Q). q = clamp(round(x/s) + z, 0, Q). z makes zero exactly representable; rounding z can shift the endpoints slightly.
ql.scale.round: round chooses the nearest integer, with half-way ties toward +∞ in this experiment. clamp bounds the code to the interval. Error is defined as e = x̂ − x. Outside the range, clipping error dominates; inside, rounding error remains.
ql.scale.caveat: With 4-bit symmetric and x = 1.25: s = 2/7, q = 4, x̂ = 8/7 ≈ 1.1429. This is a teaching convention; real formats may use other code ranges, rounding modes or nonlinear codebooks.
ql.scale.aria: Quantization levels, original value and dequantized value
ql.scale.out: b = {{bits}}; s = {{s}}; z = {{z}}; code range [{{lo}}, {{hi}}]. round(x/s) + z = {{raw}} → q = {{q}}. x̂ = {{hat}}; e = {{error}}. {{clipped}}
ql.scale.unclipped: No clamping of the integer code.
ql.groups.title: Groups, outliers and error
ql.groups.intro: One scale for a whole tensor is simple but can be set by one extreme value. Group-wise quantization splits values into smaller groups with their own scales. Here we use symmetric 4-bit with q ∈ [−7, 7] and s_g = max|x_g|/7.
ql.groups.example: The vector is [0.12, −0.18, 0.24, −0.30, 0.15, −0.21, 0.27, o]. Increase outlier o and compare group sizes 8, 4 and 2. Dashed boundaries show which values share a scale; paired bars show original and reconstruction.
ql.groups.storage: Smaller groups require more stored scales. Here count 8 × 4 bits for codes plus one 16-bit scale per group. Metadata, padding and packing can change the actual size.
ql.groups.caveat: MSE = the mean of (x̂ − x)² measures numerical error, not task quality. Smaller groups can reduce error in this example but do not guarantee better quality or lower latency in general.
ql.groups.aria: Original and dequantized bars with group boundaries and scales
ql.groups.small: Zoom on |x| ≤ 0.4; the outlier is marked
ql.groups.out: Group size {{size}}; scales: {{scales}}. MSE = {{mse}}. Codes: 32 bits + scales: {{meta}} bits = {{total}} bits ({{bytes}} bytes), versus 128 bits for 8 × 16-bit values.
ql.cal.title: Calibration without data leakage
ql.cal.intro: Post-training quantization, PTQ, adapts an already trained model. Some methods use calibration examples to select activation ranges or sensitivity-aware weight approximations. Simple weight min/max quantization may need no data calibration; dynamic activation quantization estimates ranges at runtime.
ql.cal.fit.title: Fit without peeking at the test
ql.cal.fit.1: Collect representative calibration prompts: languages, domains, lengths, chat format and challenging inputs. Preserve privacy and document selection.
ql.cal.fit.2: Choose scales, clipping thresholds and method using calibration and separate validation. Do not confuse this with an untouched test set.
ql.cal.fit.3: Save model version, tokenizer, method, bit width, group size and calibration selection so that conversion is reproducible.
ql.cal.test.title: Evaluate generalization
ql.cal.test.1: Run the locked candidate on a separate test set. If you reselect the method after seeing the test result, the test has effectively become validation data.
ql.cal.test.2: Compare against the unquantized baseline on the same examples and several relevant tasks, including minority languages and long contexts.
ql.cal.test.3: Check exact and near duplicates between splits. Shared documents or task templates can leak even without identical rows.
ql.cal.outliers: Outliers create a choice: wider ranges preserve extremes but give coarser steps for common values. Clipping can reduce mean error but damage important rare signals. Representative data helps expose this trade-off; it does not remove it.
ql.cal.caveat: Quantization-aware training, QAT, simulates quantization error during training and differs from PTQ. Neither calibration nor QAT proves quality is preserved on all future inputs.
ql.eval.title: Weights, activations and measurement
ql.eval.wo.changes: Weights are stored with 4 bits; activations use a 16-bit format. Compute and accumulation precision depend on the kernel.
ql.eval.wo.check: Memory savings including scales and packing; dequantization cost and support for your hardware.
ql.eval.wa.changes: Both are encoded with 8 bits. Activation scales may be statically calibrated or dynamic; accumulation may use higher precision.
ql.eval.wa.check: Activation outliers, conversion costs and compatible low-precision kernels. The label alone does not specify the full execution path.
ql.eval.kv: KV-cache quantization is another separate choice; W4A16 does not automatically imply a 4-bit KV cache. Model-file size, GPU memory and peak memory are different metrics.
ql.eval.protocol.1: Lock baseline and candidate: same model origin, tokenizer, prompt format, test data and generation settings. Measure quality with task metrics and loss/perplexity (perplexity = exp of mean loss) where relevant.
ql.eval.protocol.2: Warm up and repeat on the same hardware and server version. Vary prompt length, response length and concurrency; report TTFT, ITL, throughput, p50/p95 latency and peak memory.
ql.eval.protocol.3: Check that the intended kernel and quantization format are actually used. Report quality changes and uncertainty alongside performance; select for workload requirements, not bit count alone.
ql.eval.caveat: Smaller weight storage can help memory-bound workloads but does not guarantee lower latency. Kernel support, batch size, activations and conversion work can change the outcome. These offline visuals run no model and are not GPU benchmarks.
mod.quantization.name: Quantization in practice
mod.quantization.desc: From scales and integers to groups, calibration and fair measurement.
mod.quantization.lead: Save bits without confusing numerical error, task quality and performance.
mod.quantization.goal.1: Compute quantization and dequantization with scale, zero point and clipping.
mod.quantization.goal.2: Explain group size, outliers and calibration leakage.
mod.quantization.goal.3: Distinguish weight and activation precision and plan a quality and latency comparison.
mod.quantization.key.1: Dequantization gives x̂ = s(q − z). Bit width, range, rounding and clipping determine numerical error.
mod.quantization.key.2: Group scales cost metadata but limit which values an outlier affects. Calibration is fitting, not an independent test.
mod.quantization.key.3: Weight-only, activations and KV cache are separate choices. Verify quality, memory and latency for your workload.
trn.quiz.update.q: Which SGD update follows from w = 1, g = −2 and η = 0.5?
trn.quiz.update.o1: w′ = 0; subtract the step size regardless of sign
trn.quiz.update.o3: w′ = 3; always go directly to the minimum
trn.quiz.update.o4: w′ = −1; use the gradient without η
trn.quiz.update.e: w′ = w − ηg = 1 − 0.5 × (−2) = 2. L goes from 2 to 0.5 for this parabola, not for every possible loss.
trn.quiz.sft.q: What does masking instruction tokens in the SFT loss mean?
trn.quiz.sft.o1: The instruction is also removed from context
trn.quiz.sft.o2: The instruction is replaced by the model’s guess
trn.quiz.sft.o3: The instruction remains as context but contributes no direct target-position loss
trn.quiz.sft.o4: The instruction is evaluated only on the test set
trn.quiz.sft.e: The mask selects positions that contribute to loss. It need not remove text from the model’s input.
trn.quiz.preference.q: At fixed β > 0, what does a lower DPO loss for a response pair show?
trn.quiz.preference.o1: A higher reference-adjusted margin for chosen versus rejected response
trn.quiz.preference.o2: A guarantee that the chosen response is factually true
trn.quiz.preference.o3: A lower explicit KL term in this displayed loss value
trn.quiz.preference.o4: A greater probability for every token in both responses
trn.quiz.preference.e: At fixed β > 0, −ln σ(βm) decreases as m increases. This concerns the preference objective, not whether the preference is true or unbiased.
trn.quiz.lora.q: Which statement holds for row-vector LoRA in the QLoRA example?
trn.quiz.lora.o1: A has [r, 6] and B has [4, r] in the product xAB
trn.quiz.lora.o2: All base weights and gradients must be stored in 4 bits
trn.quiz.lora.o3: The adapter changes the number of output dimensions
trn.quiz.lora.o4: A [6, r] and B [r, 4] train; quantized W stays frozen
trn.quiz.lora.e: x [1, 6] × A [6, r] × B [r, 4] gives [1, 4], the same as xW. QLoRA quantizes base storage but does not require 4-bit adapters.
ql.quiz.round.q: Symmetric 4-bit: s = 2/7, z = 0, x = 1.25. What are q and x̂?
ql.quiz.round.e: x/s = 4.375 rounds to 4 within [−7, 7]. Dequantization gives (2/7) × 4 = 8/7.
ql.quiz.group.q: What trade-off is shown when the same 8 values are split into smaller quantization groups?
ql.quiz.group.o1: Fewer scales are stored but the outlier affects more values
ql.quiz.group.o2: All group sizes must give the same reconstruction
ql.quiz.group.o3: More scales are stored but fewer values share the outlier’s scale
ql.quiz.group.o4: The number of bits per weight code changes automatically
ql.quiz.group.e: Group size changes how many values share a scale. Codes remain 4-bit; metadata grows with the number of groups.
ql.quiz.leak.q: After seeing the test result you reselect the clipping threshold to improve that same test. How should the test set now be treated?
ql.quiz.leak.o1: As validation data; a new untouched test set is needed for independent assessment
ql.quiz.leak.o2: As an independent test because the base weights were not gradient-trained
ql.quiz.leak.o3: As calibration-free data because only one threshold changed
ql.quiz.leak.o4: As a more reliable test because the error became lower
ql.quiz.leak.e: Method and threshold selection also fit the system. The test result is no longer an untouched estimate of generalization.
ql.quiz.runtime.q: What can you infer from the label W4A16 alone?
ql.quiz.runtime.o1: That latency halves on the same GPU
ql.quiz.runtime.o2: That the KV cache uses a 4-bit format
ql.quiz.runtime.o3: That all multiplication and accumulation uses 4 bits
ql.quiz.runtime.o4: That weights have 4-bit encoding and activations a 16-bit format; actual latency must be measured
ql.quiz.runtime.e: The label distinguishes weight and activation formats. Kernel support, dequantization, batch size and workload affect real memory usage and latency.
ql.quiz.affine.q: Affine 4-bit with l = −1, u = 3 and x = 1.25: what do the experiment’s rules give?
ql.quiz.narrow.q: Why does the symmetric 2-bit experiment use only 3 levels?
ql.quiz.narrow.o1: Every symmetric 2-bit format must always have 3 levels
ql.quiz.narrow.o2: The zero point is stored instead of one of the bits
ql.quiz.narrow.o3: The convention uses q ∈ [−1, 1] and leaves the most negative signed code unused
ql.quiz.narrow.e: Q = 2^(2−1) − 1 = 1. The used codes are −1, 0, 1. This is an explicit convention, not a universal property of all 2-bit formats.
trn.gloss.gradient.def: The loss derivative with respect to parameters; describes local change, not a guarantee of global improvement.
trn.gloss.rate.def: A coefficient scaling an optimizer step; overly large steps can increase loss.
trn.gloss.sft.def: Supervised fine-tuning: training on demonstrations, often instruction–response pairs with a defined loss mask.
trn.gloss.rlhf.def: Reinforcement learning from human feedback; often a reward model from preferences followed by policy optimization.
trn.gloss.dpo.def: Direct preference optimization: a pairwise preference loss using log ratios against a reference policy in the standard recipe.
trn.gloss.kl.def: A directional measure of difference between probability distributions; can regularize policy drift.
trn.gloss.lora.def: Low-rank adaptation: freeze base weights and learn an additive low-rank update using two matrices.
trn.gloss.qlora.def: LoRA training through a frozen quantized base; adapter and compute precision are separate choices.
trn.gloss.scale.def: Step size s linking integer codes to reconstructed values in x̂ = s(q − z).
trn.gloss.zero.def: The integer code z representing real-valued zero in affine quantization.
trn.gloss.group.def: Values are split into groups with their own scales, trading numerical error against metadata.
trn.gloss.calibration.def: Fitting quantization parameters using representative examples; must be separated from independent testing.
trn.gloss.ptq.def: Post-training quantization: quantizing an already trained model, sometimes using calibration data.
trn.gloss.qat.def: Quantization-aware training: training that simulates quantization error in the computation.
trn.gloss.leakage.def: When evaluation-data information influences training or method selection, making evaluation overly optimistic.
